newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FEATURE - Future of shaken Belgium rests on knife edge.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Future of shaken Belgium rests on knife edge.

text.p: The future of Belgium, rocked to its foundations by a child rape and murder scandal, rests on a knife edge, according to historian Joel Kotek.

Active minorities in the federal nation's French and Dutch speaking communities are, for different reasons, pushing respectively for absorption by France or autonomy, writes Kotek in a contribution to "The Dutroux Affair", a new book on the country's difficulties.
But the normally silent and passive majority has shown clearly that it wants the 160-year-old nation to remain intact.

This, Kotek says, was shown last October when more than 250,000 people from all walks of life and all parts of the country marched through Brussels in support of the victims of paedophilia and against the system seen as allowing it.
The so-called White March was unprecedented in Belgian history and one which all 14 contributors to the new book agree was a catalytic event.
DEHAENE PROMISES REFORMS

Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene immediately promised sweeping reforms of the police and judicial system, but magistrate Foulek Ringelheim, another contributor to the book, warned they would probably not be enough.

The march was organised by the parents of dead and missing children after the arrest of convicted rapist Marc Dutroux in August and the subsequent rescue of two sexually abused young girls and the discovery of the bodies of four others.
Dutroux has been charged with murder, and police are still looking for at least six other missing chilrden.
But Kotek, a lecturer at Brussels Free University and at the Institute of European Studies, warned that the wishes of the silent majority may well be ignored.
"It is never, in reality, the people who make history but instead the active minorities," he wrote.

Kotek argues that the Dutch-speaking Flemings --who make up some 60 percent of the population --have never overcome their historical sense of inferiority to the French-speaking Walloons even though they are now numerically, politically and economically dominant.

This is translated into an aggressive radicalism, fostered by a small but highly-motivated minority with the result that the teaching of French is dying out in Flemish schools and a latent separatist movement is growing.

This in turn has been fostered by political woes with allegations of sexual misconduct and corruption that have beset Belgium's centre-left coalition government in recent months, weakening its grip and prompting opposition calls for it to stand down.

At the same time, the Walloons, whose language was that of the ruling aristocracy when Belgium was founded but who now find themselves economically and politically marginalised, fear being overwhelmed and treat their Flemish cousins with deep distrust.

"In many respects, you cannot look at Belgium today without thinking of ex-Yugoslavia. That is to say a state less federal than an accumulation of frustrations, in short a state where each of the components has the impression of being the other's dupe," Kotek wrote.
"It is far from sure that the country's unity, already badly compromised, will be able to survive the incessant buffeting by a few, well organised and very determined, minorities," he added.
However, it may be premature to write the country's obituary.
MAJORITY FAVOURS REMAINING BELGIAN
Two opinion polls late last year showed that an overwhelming majority in both linguistic camps favoured remaining Belgian -- particularly among the younger generation.

Kotek also noted that the Belgian tradition of finding a compromise solution to problems gave some hope that the cultural, political and economic time bomb might be defused before it blew the country apart.
"We are in an extraordinarily turbulent phase," wrote lawyer Marc Uyttendaele, another contributor to the book -- which is being published only in French.
